%md
## Overview

In this module we demonstrate how to create and apply user-defined functions.


## User-Defined Functions

* It is relatively easy to create and apply a user-defined function (UDF)
    * Define a Python function that operates on a row of data
    * Register the Python function as a UDF and specify the return type
    * Apply the UDF as if it were a built-in function

* Python and any required packages must be installed on the worker nodes
    * It is possible to distribute required packages via Spark

* Built-in functions are more efficient than user-defined functions
    * Use built-in functions when available
    * Create user-defined functions only when necessary

* User-defined function are inefficient because of the following:
    * A Python process must be started alongside each executor
    * Data must be converted between Java and Python types
    * Data must be transferred between the Java and Python processes

* To improve the performance of a UDF:
    * Use the [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) platform 
    * Use a vectorized UDF (see the `pandas_udf` function)
    * Rewrite the UDF in Scala or Java

%md
# Setup
---

paragraphs.title: Read the raw ride data from HDF and clean it
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

rides = spark.read.csv("/duocar/raw/rides/", header=True, inferSchema=True)

# Cast `date_time` to a timestamp:
from pyspark.sql.functions import col
rides_clean = rides.withColumn("date_time", col("date_time").cast("timestamp"))

%md
# Lesson
---

%md
## Example 1: Hour of Day

paragraphs.title: Define the Python function
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

import datetime
def hour_of_day(timestamp):
  return timestamp.hour

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md The Spark `TimestampType` corresponds to Python `datetime.datetime` objects. ### Issues with User-Defined Functions (UDFs) - **Serialization and Deserialization (Python / JVM)**: - Spark performs data processing within a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) process. - When executing pure Python code (such as a Python UDF), data must be converted from the JVM’s internal format into a Python-compatible format, processed row-by-row, and then converted back to be returned to the JVM. - This overhead negatively impacts performance and can become a significant bottleneck. - **Row-by-Row Processing**: - Conventional PySpark UDFs process elements one by one, failing to take advantage of Spark’s Catalyst query optimizer or CPU-level vectorized instructions.
- **Memory Management in Zeppelin**: - In Zeppelin, Python cells share a local interpreter. - If a UDF attempts to collect large volumes of data using `.collect()` or utilizes heavy libraries (such as SciPy or NumPy) inefficiently on local collections, it can exhaust the interpreter’s memory, leading to an "Out of Memory" error. ### Solutions and Best Practices - **Use Pandas UDFs / Vectorized UDFs (PyArrow)** - Instead of native Python UDFs, it is better to use Pandas UDFs. - These leverage Apache Arrow to transfer data in bulk between Java and Python, processing Pandas Series in batches (vectorized execution) and achieving performance gains of 10x to 100x.
- **Example:** ```python import pandas as pd from pyspark.sql.functions import pandas_udf from scipy.stats import norm # Define a vectorized Pandas UDF for the probability density function (PDF) @pandas_udf("double") def calculate_pandas_udf(series_x: pd.Series) -> pd.Series: # Process the entire data block in a vectorized manner using NumPy/SciPy return pd.Series(norm.pdf(series_x, loc=0, scale=1)) # Apply directly to the DataFrame df = df.withColumn("pdf_resultado", calcular_pdf_pandas(df["valor"])) ```

paragraphs.title: Test the Python function
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

dt = datetime.datetime(2017, 7, 21, 5, 51, 10)

print('Hora del día:', hour_of_day(dt))

paragraphs.title: Register the Python function as a UDF
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Necessary for use, for example, in Spark SQL or for accessing the Hive metastore,
# and also to make the function global so that it can be used in any pipeline.

from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
hour_of_day_udf = udf(hour_of_day, returnType=IntegerType())

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
We must explicitly specify the return type otherwise it defaults to `StringType`.

paragraphs.title: Apply the UDF
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

rides_clean \
  .select("date_time", hour_of_day_udf("date_time")) \
  .show(5, truncate=False)

paragraphs.title: Use the UDF to compute the number of rides by hour of day
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

rides_clean \
  .select(hour_of_day_udf("date_time").alias("hour_of_day")) \
  .groupBy("hour_of_day") \
  .count() \
  .orderBy("hour_of_day") \
  .show(25)

%md
## Example 2: Great-Circle Distance

The [great-circle distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great-circle_distance) is the shortest distance between two points on the surface of a sphere. 
In this example we create a user-defined function to compute the [haversine approximation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haversine_formula) to the great-circle distance between the ride origin and destination.

paragraphs.title: Define the haversine function
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from math import radians, sin, cos, sqrt, asin
def haversine(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
  """
  Return the haversine approximation to the great-circle distance between two
  points (in meters).
  """
  R = 6372.8 # Earth radius in kilometers
 
  dLat = radians(lat2 - lat1)
  dLon = radians(lon2 - lon1)

  lat1 = radians(lat1)
  lat2 = radians(lat2)
 
  a = sin(dLat / 2.0)**2 + cos(lat1) * cos(lat2) * sin(dLon / 2.0)**2
  c = 2.0 * asin(sqrt(a))
 
  return R * c * 1000.0

paragraphs.title: Note
paragraphs.text:
%md
We have made some minor changes to the code  at [rosettacode.org](http://rosettacode.org/wiki/Haversine_formula#Python) to make it integer proof.

paragraphs.title: Register the Python function as a UDF
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
haversine_udf = udf(haversine, returnType=DoubleType())

paragraphs.title: Apply the haversine UDF
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

distances = rides \
  .withColumn("haversine_approximation", haversine_udf("origin_lat", "origin_lon", "dest_lat", "dest_lon")) \
  .select("distance", "haversine_approximation")
distances.show(5)

paragraphs.title: We expect the haversine approximation to be less than the ride distance
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

distances \
  .select((col("haversine_approximation") > col("distance")).alias("haversine > distance")) \
  .groupBy("haversine > distance") \
  .count() \
  .show()

# The null values correspond to cancelled rides:
rides.filter(col("cancelled") == 1).count()

# The true values reflect the fact that the haversine formula is only an approximation to the great-circle distance:
distances.filter(col("haversine_approximation") > col("distance")).show(5)

paragraphs.title: 1- Create a UDF that extracts the day of the week from a timestamp column
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

# Define the Python function:
import datetime
def day_of_week(timestamp):
  return timestamp.weekday()

# Register the Python function as a UDF: 
from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
day_of_week_udf = udf(day_of_week, returnType=IntegerType())

# Apply the UDF:
rides_clean \
  .select("date_time", day_of_week_udf("date_time")) \
  .show(5, truncate=False)

paragraphs.title: Hint
paragraphs.text:
%md
Use the [weekday](https://docs.python.org/2/library/datetime.html#datetime.datetime.weekday) method of the Python `datetime` class.

paragraphs.title: 2 - Use the UDF to compute the number of rides by day of week
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

rides_clean \
  .withColumn("day_of_week", day_of_week_udf("date_time")) \
  .groupBy("day_of_week") \
  .count() \
  .orderBy("day_of_week") \
  .show()

paragraphs.title: 3 - Use the built-in function `dayofweek` to compute the number of rides by day of week
paragraphs.text:
%pyspark

from pyspark.sql.functions import dayofweek
rides_clean \
  .withColumn("dayofweek", dayofweek("date_time")) \
  .groupBy("dayofweek") \
  .count() \
  .orderBy("dayofweek") \
  .show()

%md
# Result
**You have now:** Learned how to use UDFs to transform DataFrames
